decision.summary: 107 of 111 findings are evidence-backed; 4 were insufficient and recorded for follow-up.

findings.statement: Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): AMD is working with SiFive to tune its open-source ROCm AI software for RISC-V datacenter servers, with initial technical demonstrations showing the ROCm stack running on SiFive RISC-V hardware for datacenter AI workloads.

Broadcom develops custom accelerators or XPUs, which are application-specific integrated circuits built to individual customer specifications for AI and high-performance computing. These custom silicon products serve hyperscalers, companies with AI frontier models, and system integrators, and are sometimes used in racks or systems.

Broadcom partners with hyperscale cloud providers to co-design custom AI accelerator chips tailored to each customer's workloads. Several hyperscaler custom silicon programs built with Broadcom have moved from research projects to production hardware, shifting a growing share of training and inference to custom chips.
Broadcom announced an extended partnership with Meta on June 9, 2026, to deploy technology supporting Meta's custom silicon MTIA.
Broadcom has secured over $10 billion of orders for AI racks based on its XPUs from a qualified customer.

Broadcom's AI semiconductor solutions include Ethernet switching and routing silicon, Ethernet NICs, physical layer devices (PHYs), and optical components, as well as racks and systems based on its XPUs.
Broadcom offers open, standards-based Ethernet NIC and switching solutions designed to resolve connectivity bottlenecks in AI data centers where compute bandwidth and cluster sizes grow rapidly.
Broadcom provides custom AI accelerators and Ethernet-based AI networking chips designed for large hyperscale customers.
Broadcom: Meta deploys Broadcom technology to support its custom silicon MTIA under an extended partnership announced on June 9, 2026.
Broadcom, Apollo, and Blackstone established a landmark strategic platform on April 14, 2026, to accelerate more than 20 gigawatts of global AI deployments.
Broadcom plans to deploy racks of AI accelerators and network systems starting in the second half of 2026, supported by over $10 billion of XPU-based AI rack orders from a qualified customer.

Google makes Cloud TPUs available to external Google Cloud customers: Compute Engine provides access to CPUs, GPUs, and Cloud TPUs (S13), and Google Cloud lists "Optimize with TPU" among the delivery methods available to external users (S4). The supplied evidence does not specify which TPU accelerator generations are offered.

Google Cloud offers A4 VMs powered by Blackwell B200 GPUs in preview (S1) and A4X VMs built on GB200 NVL72 systems containing 72 B200 GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs (S2). The evidence does not include pricing for these Blackwell-based instances or for TPU-based instances.

Intel Gaudi 2 AI accelerator was introduced in 2022 and is built on a 7nm process. It is supported by the Intel Gaudi software suite, which integrates the PyTorch framework, and is purpose-built for deep learning workloads including large language models, chatbots, and retrieval augmented generation. The accelerator enables organizations to scale AI workloads with an open, vendor-agnostic platform.

Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator is manufactured on TSMC 5nm process technology and supports PCIe 5.0, providing improved area density and power efficiency over Gaudi 2. It delivers more than 2x FP8 GEMM FLOPs and more than 4x BF16 GEMM FLOPs compared to Gaudi 2, with 1.5x faster HBM bandwidth and 1.33x larger HBM capacity. The accelerator targets state-of-the-art datacenter performance for generative AI workloads including large language models and diffusion models.

Intel Gaudi 3 AI Accelerator PCIe Card (HL-338) is available as a standard PCIe Gen 5.0 add-in card in a full-height, dual-slot form factor measuring 10.5 inches with a 600W card-level TDP. The card features 128GB of HBM2e memory with 3.7 TB/s total throughput, 8 MME engines, and 64 fully programmable Tensor Processor Cores. It is designed for inference and fine-tuning of AI models and can be integrated into new or existing AI server designs.

Intel positions Xeon processors as handling every AI workload from traditional ML inference to frontier AI without GPU lock-in. Intel Xeon 6787P (2S) delivers 4x throughput on Speech Recognition (OpenAI Whisper) and 2.2x throughput on Computer Vision (RetinaNet) in MLPerf v5.1 inference benchmarks. Intel Xeon is described as the most deployed host CPU for AI systems, available across a wide range of AI systems from leading OEMs.

Intel positions Xeon as the leading host CPU for AI accelerated systems, with DGX Rubin NVL8 platform leveraging Intel Xeon 6 processors as the host CPU. Intel co-validates Xeon CPUs with GPUs on DGX, HGX, and MGX reference designs, and Intel will build custom x86 CPUs with NVLink for integration into AI infrastructure platforms.

Intel's workload placement guidance states that traditional AI (ML, DL) runs best on the CPU built for AI, while frontier AI (LLMs, training) runs best on GPU systems with Intel Xeon as host. For generative AI (SLMs, LLMs), customers can choose either GPU or Intel Xeon based on business needs, and agentic AI requires a balance of both Intel Xeon and GPU in an optimal ratio.

Intel: On 5th generation Intel Xeon processors, the NuPIC inference platform achieved over two orders of magnitude improvement in throughput on CPUs enabled for Intel AMX compared to previous-generation CPUs. It outperformed a data center GPU by up to 17x on BERT-Large inference at batch size 1, and the solution does not require batching for high performance, making it suitable for real-time applications.

Intel Foundry operates as the world's first systems foundry designed for the AI era, offering full-stack design and fab services plus global packaging and test facilities. It manufactures for multiple architectures including ARM, RISC-V, x86, and custom ASICs, supporting major IP portfolios and ecosystem partners for customer chip designs. The foundry provides access to Intel technologies for memory systems, interconnects, cooling, thermal management, networking, and software.

Intel: Microsoft is a confirmed Intel Foundry customer, with CEO Satya Nadella announcing that Microsoft has chosen a chip design it plans to produce on the Intel 18A process. The announcement was made at Intel Foundry Direct Connect in February 2024, where ecosystem partners including Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens, and Ansys outlined validated tools and design flows for customer designs.

Intel 18A is on track for production in 2025, with lead products Panther Lake and Clearwater Forest already powered on and booted operating systems. The first external customer is expected to tape out on Intel 18A in the first half of 2025, indicating foundry availability for external AI chip designs beyond Intel's own products.

Intel Gaudi 3 AI Accelerator is optimized for large-scale generative AI and features 64 Tensor processor cores, eight matrix multiplication engines, 128 GB of HBM2e memory for training and inference, and 24 200 Gigabit Ethernet ports for scalable networking. It offers seamless compatibility with the PyTorch framework and advanced Hugging Face transformer and diffuser models. The product launched at an event on September 24, 2024, with Gaudi 3 clusters beginning to roll out the following quarter for large-scale production deployments.

Intel: IBM Cloud is the first cloud service provider to make Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators available to customers, marking the first major commercial deployment of Gaudi 3. Through the Intel-IBM collaboration, clients can cost-effectively test, innovate, and deploy generative AI solutions using Gaudi 3 as a service. Select customers also gained early access to Gaudi 3 for validating AI model deployments.

Intel: A standard AI kit including eight Intel Gaudi 2 accelerators with a universal baseboard is offered to system providers at $65,000, estimated to be one-third the cost of comparable competitive platforms. A kit including eight Intel Gaudi 3 accelerators with a universal baseboard lists at $125,000, estimated to be two-thirds the cost of comparable competitive platforms. Gaudi 2 is commercially available, while Gaudi 3 pricing was announced at Computex 2024 ahead of its September 2024 launch.

findings.statement: Intel positions Xeon 6 processors with P-cores as capable of efficiently handling the majority of non-generative AI workloads used in the enterprise without requiring costly, dedicated GPU systems. The processors can reduce total cost of ownership by consolidating servers and reducing power consumption in the data center. Intel also describes 4th Gen Xeon processors as enabling a single universal AI system for data pre-processing, model training, and deployment.

Intel Xeon 6 processors with P-cores deliver up to 2x better AI inference performance compared to AMD EPYC processors and up to 44% lower TCO running a BERT-Large LLM workload compared to AMD EPYC. The processors feature integrated AI acceleration in every core, increased core count, and double the memory bandwidth. Intel Xeon 6 launched with Performance-cores in September 2024, doubling performance for AI and HPC workloads compared to its predecessor.

Intel remains the only CPU vendor to submit MLPerf results, with 4th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors submitting results for ResNet50, RetinaNet, BERT, and DLRM dcnv2. The MLPerf results demonstrate deep learning training performance for customers building Xeon-based servers for AI workloads. Intel Gaudi2 is one of only three accelerator solutions with MLPerf results, and one of two commercially available.

Intel Foundry will produce an AI fabric chip for Amazon Web Services on Intel 18A as part of a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar framework covering product and wafers. Intel also produces a custom Xeon 6 chip on Intel 3 for AWS, building on an existing partnership under which Intel produces Xeon Scalable processors for AWS. The companies expect deep engagement on additional designs spanning Intel 18A, Intel 18AP, and Intel 14A.

Intel 18A is customer-ready, with Panther Lake and Clearwater Forest processors powered on and booting operating systems. The first external customer is expected to tape out on Intel 18A in the first half of next year. Intel Foundry is bringing together components needed to design next-generation AI solutions for foundry customers.

Cisco Systems: Cisco's Silicon One G300 switch chip is designed for massive data centers to help AI training and inference chips communicate over hundreds of thousands of links, with automatic traffic re-routing around network problems within microseconds, and is expected to go on sale in the second half of the year.

Cisco Systems: Cisco's AI-centric networking strength is positioned to capture share in the AI switch market, where Ethernet is forecast to account for up to 90% of growth as hyperscaler AI clusters scale out.

Cisco Systems: Cisco is integrating its Silicon One silicon into an AI-optimized Ethernet networking platform, with Cisco as the only partner silicon supported in that platform's solutions, to deliver a unified architecture for AI-ready data center networks.

Cisco Systems: Cisco's Silicon One G300 chip launch is positioned as competing against rival AI networking chip suppliers for a share of the AI infrastructure spending boom, indicating direct competition at the AI networking chip level.

Cisco Systems: Cisco reported surpassing its fiscal year 2025 goal of $1 billion in hyperscaler AI networking gear orders in its third quarter ended April 26, indicating hyperscaler demand for Cisco AI networking equipment.

Google offers Cloud TPU v5e accelerators to external customers through Google Cloud. The vLLM-TPU inference stack is explicitly tailored to Trillium and v5e TPU generations, and v5e is listed as available on a hyperscaler for TPU-based workloads. Customers can use these TPUs for training and inference workloads on Google Cloud.

Google offers Ironwood, identified as TPU v7, with 4,614 TFLOPs per chip, 192GB of HBM3e memory, and pod scaling to 9,216 chips delivering 42.5 exaFLOPS. Ironwood features an inference-first design and ICI interconnect at 9.6 Tb/s per chip. This is a seventh-generation TPU accelerator in Google's lineup.

Google provides the JAX AI stack for Cloud TPUs, consisting of core libraries JAX, Flax, Optax, Orbax, and Grain. JAX provides accelerator-oriented array computation with JIT, grad, vmap, and pmap transformations. The stack is designed as an end-to-end open-source platform for machine learning at extreme scales on TPUs and GPUs.

Google's TPU software stack relies on XLA, a domain-specific hardware-independent compiler that supports TPU, CPU, and GPU devices, and Pathways, a distributed runtime for orchestrating computation across tens of thousands of chips. XLA performs whole-program analysis, operation fusion, and memory layout optimization. Pathways handles fault tolerance, recovery, and automation for large-scale training runs.

Google: TPUs execute compiled XLA programs rather than CUDA kernels, and JAX compiles to XLA natively. This gives JAX a structural advantage on TPUs that CUDA-based frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow on GPU cannot fully replicate. Google's Gemini, PaLM 2, and Gemma models are trained in JAX on TPU pods at scales involving thousands of chips.

Google open-sourced TorchTPU, co-built with Meta, allowing users to run existing PyTorch code on TPUs by changing device=\"cuda\" to \"tpu\". It works with Hugging Face (device_map=\"tpu\"), vLLM, and SGLang with minimal code rewrites. This provides a PyTorch-native path to TPU hardware.

Google's TPUs are optimized for JAX and TensorFlow, while PyTorch support is available through PyTorch/XLA but is described as limited and less stable. TPUs handle standard neural network operations efficiently but struggle with custom kernels or mixed-framework workloads. This contrasts with the broad framework support available on general-purpose GPUs.
